query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐component concentrated alloys, nanoscale fluctuations in local chemical ordering (SRO) create spatial variations in the generalized planar fault (or stacking fault) energy that pin dislocations along irregular, wavy paths. This increased dislocation barrier delays dislocation motion and promotes work hardening, thereby governing the alloy’s high strength and enhanced ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A well‐annealed multi‐component concentrated alloy (e.g., a CrCoNi or similar high-/medium‐entropy alloy) exhibiting significant local chemical order (SRO) and associated fault energy fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Prepare a controlled set of alloy samples where SRO is varied via processing: one set processed (e.g., via low-temperature annealing) to promote stable SRO and another set processed (e.g., by severe plastic deformation or high-temperature annealing) to suppress or randomize SRO.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at ambient (and optionally cryogenic) temperatures where dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates, with identical grain sizes and microstructural backgrounds aside from SRO variations.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering (SRO) and the resulting spatial fluctuations in the generalized stacking/fault energy landscape.
generation.mechanism: The SRO-induced fault energy fluctuations introduce ‘hard atomic motifs’ that pin moving dislocations and force them into irregular, wavy glide paths. This enhances the activation barrier for dislocation motion, results in more effective dislocation storage, and increases work hardening, thereby elevating yield strength and delaying local deformation localization or necking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline with suppressed SRO, samples with pronounced SRO will exhibit higher yield strengths, greater work hardening rates, and display dislocation patterns with more pronounced waviness or pinning features. Microscopic examination (e.g., via TEM) will reveal concentrated zones of pinned or wavy dislocation segments aligning with regions of SRO.
generation.baseline: An identically composed alloy processed to minimize SRO (e.g., by high-temperature annealing) so that the generalized fault energy is closer to a uniform value.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in multi-component concentrated (high-/medium-entropy) alloys with significant atomic size/chemistry differences leading to measurable SRO; other strengthening mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary effects) are controlled for by ensuring similar microstructures across comparisons.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports SRO’s role in modifying dislocation behavior, quantifying its contribution versus other lattice-distortion or defect-based mechanisms remains challenging. Additionally, the sensitivity of fault-energy fluctuations to processing conditions introduces some uncertainty in precise quantitative effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same multi-component alloy: one set processed to enhance SRO (via controlled low-temperature annealing) and a second set processed to randomize SRO (via high-temperature treatment or severe plastic deformation). Perform uniaxial tensile tests under identical conditions. Characterize the dislocation structures using TEM and assess local SRO using appropriate diffraction or atom probe techniques.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress from tensile tests
Work hardening rate and strain to failure
Dislocation density and morphology (e.g., degree of waviness or pinning) via TEM
Quantitative metrics of SRO (e.g., using atom probe tomography or diffuse scattering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with enhanced SRO do not show a statistically reproducible increase in yield strength and work hardening rate, nor exhibit significantly different (e.g., more pinned or wavy) dislocation patterns compared to samples with randomized SRO, then the hypothesis that SRO-induced fault energy fluctuations govern the strength and deformation behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceComplex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with multi elements in equiatomic ratios are exotic alloys but what governs their strength is currently not clearly understood. This work has proven the prime origin of strength in CCAs as arising from the fluctuations (not the averaged value) of the shear-fault energy, which is an important feature of CCAs unrecognized beforehand. Through identification of the local hard atomic motifs far beyond the traditional concept of the globally averaged short-range ordering parameters, this work has unfolded the physical basis of strength in CCAs and provides important clues for designing high-strength CCAs by focusing on the alloy composition to produce large fault-energy fluctuations. Local chemical short-range ordering (SRO) and spatial fluctuations of planar fault energy are important features of multi-element and metastable complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). We report multi-component high-entropy materials as extraordinarily robust diffusion barriers and clarify the highly suppressed interdiffusion kinetics in the multi-component materials from structural and thermodynamic perspectives. The failures of six alloy barriers with different numbers of elements, from unitary Ti to senary TiTaCrZrAlRu, against the interdiffusion of Cu and Si were characterized, and experimental results indicated that, with more elements incorporated, the failure temperature of the barriers increased from 550 to 900°C. The activation energy of Cu diffusion through the alloy barriers was determined to increase from 110 to 163 kJ/mole. Mechanistic analyses suggest that, structurally, severe lattice distortion strains and a high packing density caused by different atom sizes, and, thermodynamically, a strengthened cohesion provide a total increase of 55 kJ/mole in the activation energy of substitutional Cu diffusion, and are believed to be the dominant factors of suppressed interdiffusion kinetics through the multi-component barrier materials.

High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution.
